chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, and Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, all of them, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the slave girl who belongs to a man, whom he has sexual relations with, and she gives birth, and she attaches the child to him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Does the man accuse her, or does his family accuse her?' I said: 'As for apparent [evidence], no.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Then the child is necessitated upon him.'

key_terms.تَخْرُج: She gives birth (literally: she comes out)
key_terms.يُطِيفُ بِهَا: He has sexual relations with her (literally: circles around her)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on paternity of a child born to a slave girl if the owner disputes it?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the principle of 'Istibra' (presumption of paternity) in Shia jurisprudence, where a master's ownership of a slave girl creates a legal presumption that any child she bears belongs to him unless explicitly disputed. The narration highlights the procedural nuance that mere accusation by the master or his family is sufficient to trigger the attribution of lineage, provided there is no external evidence contradicting this claim. This ruling underscores the importance of paternity disputes in determining inheritance and marital eligibility within the early Islamic community.
